create.name: Rashid Hughes
create.bio:
Rashid Hughes is a mindfulness and yoga teacher who links contemplative practice with restorative justice and community care. He studied music and then divinity at Howard University, holds certifications as a mindfulness teacher and a yoga instructor, and has been training to serve as a fire pujari. His teaching centres on R.E.S.T., his own approach to meditation: relaxing attention, letting go of striving, sensing silence and trusting awareness, so that sitting becomes a way of resting in one's natural state rather than another task to manage.

In 2019 he co-founded the Heart Refuge Mindfulness Community in Washington, DC, which offers free weekly practice groups grounded in the experiences of Black, Indigenous and people of colour, and he leads its sessions for men and masculine-identifying practitioners. Alongside this he works in DC schools as a restorative justice facilitator, building circles for accountability and community. He writes for Mindful, Lion's Roar and the Garrison Institute on rest, loneliness, compassion and haiku as meditation, and shares recorded talks on grief, brokenness and freedom.

free_resources.title: R.E.S.T.: A Guided Practice for the Tired & Weary
free_resources.description: A guided practice published by Mindful that walks through the four steps of his R.E.S.T. approach. It invites the reader to rest in awareness instead of working to calm down.

free_resources.title: How Writing Three Lines of Poetry Can Open Your Heart
free_resources.description: An article on writing haiku as a form of meditation, with a simple way to begin. Linked from his published-work page.

free_resources.title: Working with Loneliness on the Contemplative Path
free_resources.description: A Lion's Roar piece on listening to loneliness during a contemplative life and turning towards connection with others.

free_resources.title: What to Do When Aggression Masquerades as Compassion
free_resources.description: A short teaching on using mindfulness to notice when what feels like compassion is really aggression.

free_resources.title: The Great Bypass: Resting in the Aliveness of Being
free_resources.description: An essay for the Garrison Institute that asks who we are at the level of being, and how resting there changes practice.
